blocks.x: Let's see, we're recording today in room 104, History Building. What's today's date? I forgot. Day 8? June 8th. June 8th, 1960. And who are we interviewing today? Tell your name.
Tony Fugero.

Okay, Paul? Paul Crawford. He's running the machine, and I'm Dick Allen. Okay, we've got everybody identified now for the secretary. Tony, first thing I'd like to know is, when were you born and where?

Well, I was born in New Orleans in 1900, April 25th. And I started my... Funny thing about music, never even had music in my brain. I always wanted to be a locomotive engineer. When I was a kid, I always fooled around engines. And I went along, and here comes around the year 1918. Instead of winding up getting a job in the railroad, I wind up being a musician. In fact, it was just born on me. I never took a lesson. I just bought a horn on Ramport Street. I never will forget that. It was a tin horn. I don't remember the make of it anymore. I didn't know it was a cornet. And the valves was rusty, and I had a wake on it. And I started blowing on that thing in one key. I always did playing a key of C. That was a big deal in them days, playing one key. In fact, in those days, the musicians just played in about two keys, C and F. Put them in another key, and they got lost. But in later years, I've played with musicians like Leonard Beisdorf. It's Johnny Beisdorf's brother. And he played in all black keys, and I didn't even know what it was, because I was only playing in this key of C, because everybody in those days tuned up in the same key. With the piano. Everybody tuned up with the piano, and we all played in the same key. Until I got mingling around in later years, about 1923 or 1924, I got to play with some pretty good musicians, like I said, Leonard Beisdorf, and Leo Addy, and the piano player, the name of Joe Gary, just did. Now, we all played a little job. I played over at the Hotsy Totsy. Then it was about a half a block from Little Club in them days. I don't know if you remember them. Well, I'm telling you, it's way back in 1924, something like that. And we used to play upstairs. This was an upstairs place, and everybody had a regular jam session. Everybody would come around in the morning when they were off, and was a piano player. He's dead now with the name of Lobosky, and Max Fink was a very noted violinist. They all used to come over there in the morning to hear this kind of music, because they were playing all that, what you call long hair music all night, and they used to like to hear this stuff. They didn't know how it came out the horns or anything else. They used to go over there, just loved it, and want to hit, and they used to get there every morning. We used to have a big jam session, and have a big cheese box for a kitty in them days. They used to just throw the money in there to hear us play.
What kind of piano player was Lobosky?

Oh, Lobosky was a fine, talented piano player. He wasn't much a jazz man, though, but I mean he was what you call a semi-jazz man. He could read and play any kind of a show that came along, but he could play some jazz too. But I mean he couldn't play like the man that featured more today, because he was a different class musician than us. In other words, he was first class musician, I'd say. Who was he playing with? Well, he was playing with Max Finkman. And there was a clarinet player. He's dead, and I can't think of his name, offhand. I don't know it.
Well, in those days,
and well, this boy here, Red Bowman, was in that outfit, I think. He was a mighty good trumpet man in them days too.
Well, Perranti talks about Lobosky as a guy he played with.
Who? Tony Perranti. Yeah, Tony Perranti played in that band. That's the one, yeah, he played. Tony and a set of clarinet played. Tony was playing most saxon them days when he was playing clarinet.
Let me see. I'm trying to think of who's the only clarinet player
in that town work. Oh, I can't think of that boy's name. No, he's...
Did he play a noodling style? Oh, he played a fine style. He played a style on the style of rap. Rap. Someone like Skaggs. Skaggs. Skaggs.
Skaggs.
Yeah. About that style of clarinet like Skaggs.

Yeah, yeah. And, uh... Well, all in all, of course, after playing around here, all them years, I made Burden Street up and down the street. Played Silver Slipper in the old days. And, uh... Played for... Played for... Loey Primer played out on Burden Street there. It's right across from the... From the... Show Bar. You know that club right across the street? I forgot the name of it. No, he was given... Years ago. And then, I... I start to hit the road then. I hit the road in about 1928. I joined... Uh... What you call... Presentation shows. Something like this.
Was that something like vaudeville?
Yeah, this is strictly a vaudeville show.
I see they got the girls there.

Yeah, well, the band is in the back, you see. So, I went into something different for a while. I was, uh... Playing mostly stage work. And, uh... Well, I did that for a long time, too. I was batted on the road, and we hit, uh... One-nighters, and... Played all over the country. But this show, this was not a show here, the Hollywood Scandals. This was a band I had down here in New Orleans. I met Jeff Riddick, and... I don't know. A couple of boys. I don't know if you know them all.
I don't know. I see Jeff right there.
But others, I don't believe I know. Uh... Billy Newburger. You don't know. He's a drummer? Yeah, he's a drummer. This is Al Bernard. This is Frank Topey.
Let's see.
He plays Frank Topey? Topey, yeah. He plays saxophone.
And this other fella here?
He's a saxophone, Marshall Farrell. That was Jeff back here, and Al Bernard.
He's the same guy that's back in town, not a bass player, huh?

Yeah. That's a band that played around here, over the river. Different spots. Well, I front that band for about three or four years. Then I come back off the road, and I went out to Pontchartrain Beach. Here's a picture here with Harry Shields. That's a terrible-looking picture, but that's the way we looked in them days. Yeah. Like we were hungry. We were on a panic. That's Harry there. That's Harry there. That's Harry there. And that's me. This fella by the name of Foster Petty was a piano player. This fella was Zito, a guitar player. This is a little Serge, you know, a little Serge. Stan Serge? Stan Serge on the drum. This guy? Yeah. This guy? Stan Serge on the drum. This guy? Yeah. This guy? This guy? This guy? Yeah. This guy? This guy? This guy? Yeah. This guy? This guy? Yeah. This guy? This guy? This Zito?
What Zito was this?

Oh, that was another Zito. That wasn't the same one. Oh, yeah. He was a guitar player. He played out the beach for a whole season out there. And then went around. So I hit the road again. I couldn't make money here, so I had to hit the road again. So I joined a couple of, we used to call them turkeys in them days, these tent shows. I think this one here. That's a Hollywood scandal. Yeah, yeah. It was a presentation show. But I've had him on here somewhere. Well, it was Jimmy Rogers. I played with him. I don't know if you remember him. The guitar player got his records, yeah. Yeah, the guitar player, yeah. From Meridian, huh? Yeah. Yeah.
I remember him.
The guitar player got his records, yeah. Yeah, the guitar player, yeah. From Meridian, huh?
Yeah.

I was looking for that shows. Well, anyhow, I hit the tent shows. And I played on the tent shows for a long time. And played weak stands. You know how that went. And I hit up around Chicago and got on an off-him circuit for a while. I wouldn't have to hit up around Chicago and got on an off-him circuit for a while. And I hit up around Chicago and got on an off-him circuit for a while. For what that showed at it. And I hit up around Chicago and got on an off-him circuit for a while. For what that showed at it. And we played on a tent shows for a long time. And I played on a tent shows for a long time. And I played weak stands. And I played weak stands. And played weak stands. And you know how that went. And I played weak stands. And you know how that went. And sometimes it got paid and sometimes it did. So I was on a panic there for a while. And I hit up around Chicago and got on an off-him circuit for a while. With that show that Hollywood Scandals. We played all around there for a while. And played in the Palace in New York. And in Chicago. Went around and played all up in that section. We were supposed to go to New England states. Where we canceled out on the count of the Union. They were trying to put the pit bands in. Like the stage bands. You know. Well I mean all them things. Work on and on. You know. And for just to know you was out of a job again. Well you was back on that panic again. What you miss. Yeah. That starvation panic. So. Now this is a slow band. And I was playing when they called it the People and Gold Collegiate. It was a band out of Bayon Rouge. A lot of college boys in them from LSU. So we'd spot up around there a while. Then we'd get back on the road again. So my life was mostly in and out of this town. Like I said I played a lot of spots. I really can't think of them all. But there's a lot of stuff from reading in here. Places that I've been around. Jumped around in. I even got a letter one time from a. About to find a letter. They, they, uh. It was from a. Call it club out in. Really. And they wanted us to come up there and play a dance. They thought you were coming? Yeah. I was the one of Penn's style.
You could have hired Jack Lane's band.

Oh I didn't know man. I had the letter here. If I could find that letter and let you read that letter. It was really funny man. It had the funnies in that. Surgeys and Wilder. I knew it was a colored club though. But the man sure wrote a nice letter and said, how much you like the band. You know, we, we were playing out here at that time. I got that letter out there. I used to broadcast over at WWL a whole lot. You know. And, uh. He wanted us to come up there and play, play that dance. But. Never did get to make that one though. But I believe I, uh, uh, uh. Would have liked of playing it. I don't know. I don't think I'd have got a kick out of that. Yeah. I'd really believe so. I'd have got a kick out of that. I could have, could have got by with it. But. Never did get up there. Well let me ask you something. Yeah. Did any of your family play music? Well, uh. No, my, my, uh.
background was mostly from my, uh, uh, mother's side.

See, I, I had a cousin, uh, that played music. He was a clarinet player. His name was Johnny Peugeot. And, uh, he played with, uh, Papa Lane's band and, uh, Uses band. We used to call it Puckeye Uses band. We used to call it Puckeye Uses band. And, uh. We used to call it Puck Iuse's band. A fellow with Glass Eye used to play cornet. And played with Fish's band in those days. He was the one who got me started in playing the band, you know, because they used to book parades. They'd have about ten men in a band. They would have six men playing and four of us was dummies. And I was one of the dummies. It started like that with a rag in my heart. I couldn't play though, but I got paid anyhow to fill the band out. In those days, that's the way they did it.
To get you started. What did your cousin say? They'd have ten men and there'd be four niggers, five dummies?

Yeah. Yeah, you see. Excuse me. He used to tell me that. He would say they had folk calling people in a plane. I said, well, I turn around and look. I said, well, I surely don't see anybody around here. Look, she called it. He said, well, they got four of them in here playing. And they'd point them out to me afterwards, you know. But I was green as grass, man. I was a big time. Boy, I thought, man, playing in that band, boy, I was something big. You know, just starting out in a band like Fisher's Band. And there was bands in Lane's Band. There was a few other bands in them days. Triangle. And, uh, oh, I tell you, man, I played with so many bands. I played with this, uh, well, I played with, uh, Chink Martinet and, uh, Paul Lionel, Elysian Field and Dauphin. It was right above the police station. I can't think of that. Near the Lusitania? Yeah, the Lusitania Hall, yeah.
Played up in there.

And there was Chink Martin and, uh, uh, a fella by the name of Tots on the drums. He's dead now. And, uh, Hogan on the guitar. Well, I believe he's dead, too. I was Chink and I was about the only one living out that outfit. And this Frank Crixton played there. And this, and this fella, Charlie Crixton, who was a brother to Frank Crixton, he played with me. I think you had sure that picture before. With the Dominoes?
Yeah, with the Dominoes.

Willie Guitars? Yeah, Willie Guitars. And Nappy? Nappy Lamar and, uh, uh, Aleister Boucher. We all used to play at Woodman Hall on a Saturday night. That was a big deal. I think we got about three dollars and a ham sandwich to play on it.
Oh, who was the piano player in that picture? Uh, Nappy's brother or something? Brother, yeah.
What's his name? Uh, uh, not, not Will, uh, oh, I can't think of him. Oh, look, it'll come down.
Yeah. And who was the drummer?
Uh, Tony of Barella. He was a candy maker at Holmes'. Barella?
Barella.
Barella.
Barella.

And, uh, it was Charlie Christen on the trombone and, uh, uh, myself, Willie Guitars played bass and lived on Music Street. He used to have a little trap, trap, door, door on the bass, you know, and we'd always wonder because he used to drink, you know, plenty. So, we'd always wonder, say, well, how the devil could he, he'd get drunk that quick? See? So, he'd carry his whiskey and a little medicine bottle, see, and that little trap door in them days in the bass. So, he'd open up the trap door and pull a bottle out and take some more medicine. He said, man, I got a terrible cold tonight. Funchest thing you know, about 10 o'clock, he was riding a bass all over the floor. Man, he was knocked out. I guess that trap door came in. Oh, that trap door, man, was something for him. I'll tell you that right now, man. He really got his kicks in that deal. Having a nice, that's a tense show we're talking about. Oh, yeah. One-nighters. We used to make, that's, that's, uh, Paul English Players. I trooped on that show for about a year.
How big a band would you have in that band?
Oh, we had six men in that band.
Any new orange guys in there besides you? All new orange guys?
No, all the rest of them from Baton Rouge and then, they had a boy from up around Mississippi. I don't know, I was the only one from him. Old Baton Rouge boy.
You had a mustache on.
Yeah, I had a mustache and a, you know, a pair of golf pants on. There was a golf in them days, too. They golfed the liquor, though. What you could get.
Well, how old were you when you had bought your hornet in the, was it a hot shop or what, where you got the hornet?

Yeah, I bought my, my horn at a place they called Uncle Joe, down on Ramport Street. Okay, $12 for it. And I started out then, it was about, I was about 20. I was about, well, I actually was, no, I was about 18 years old when I started.
And Jack Lane was still going then, huh?
Oh, he was going strong, Jack Lane. Yeah, he was, he was really starting out. And Jack Lane was, he was playing years and years before I had started.
Yeah, I wondered when he retired. I didn't know. Oh, I didn't know.

I forgot after, because I had left town. I didn't know what happened to him after that, until I saw him at the jazz club, you know? Because I was going for about five years there, one trip. I didn't think I made 109 towns in one year. Gee, I was really jumping. I'd make an overnight jump for 500 miles, and I'd leave out of Jackson, Mississippi, and jump into Jackson, Tennessee, or something like that, you know? I'd play there maybe one night or two nights, and then I was going again. I could jump up to, around Chicago, and we played Gary and Aurora and St. Charles and Jolliette, Chicago, and play around that section there. And then maybe, and then jump, jump then into Minneapolis and play around there, and then get back into South Carolina, North Carolina. Just jumping all the time. Never forget one time there, we started out in Arkansas. Oh man, that was a, you talk about a slow boat to China. It was a slow process getting, getting out of that state. We, we really was on a panic. We were on a, the show wasn't making no money. They had to charge the baggage to the hotel, and leave it there, and go to the next town, and borrow money from the show to send back to the hotel to pick up the props and all the baggage, and move it into the next town. Talking about hardships. So, these chorus gals here that you saw here, they were always hungry, you know. So I'll never forget that. This little band there, we used to travel around a little old model there ford. This guy here was named Fliver Ford. You can see he's got a little tam on, with a banjo play. His name was Fliver Ford. So, we used to travel around this little old model there ford, you know. Get, get in the town in the morning. Man, we'd be hungry, boys. This guy would say, where do we eat? Well, the boss man, he, he, he, what that, and he says, eat? He said, you all look like ducks now. You can't throw your legs up in the morning. You're worried about eating. And, he wouldn't, he wouldn't feed us that morning, man. That was the funny part about it. We were hungry. I'll never forget the time my, my wife said, what's the matter? You don't write no more. I said, well, if you send me some stamps, I'll write you. And we're charging the stamps to the hotel bills. That's right. That's how rough it was, you know. But, uh, off and all, no, we'd have a bad break. You know how it is, man. You'd get a good break. Now, that's, that same show started with a bad break. And we wound up making plenty of money with that show. And all kind of offers. With this Hollywood Scandal show. Every, everybody thought it was from Hollywood, you know. They saw it. And it, man, it made plenty of money when it got on that, Sanger circuit for a while. And we got through there. And, you know, if they're getting out of Arkansas, you know, you play these old, uh, independent houses, you know. And they just depend upon what they can get at night. And they couldn't pay the show off. So they owed you the money. So what could you do? And you had to just struggle and struggle until you hit it good. And, uh, the same as many times I played in the town for room and board and we spotted out at night. Well, we, uh, we, uh, we were sure of one thing to eat. And, uh, sleep. And we'd catch one or two or three spot jobs a week. And we had a little money in our pocket. But sometimes we made big money. Sometimes we didn't. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. well they called them cafes in them days, on Rampart Street. Him and King Oliver was playing together. Loey was playing the second trumpet. I never will forget that. And I was just starting out and I heard so much about Loey. And I went in there and heard him playing. And then in later years after he got playing good there, there was a little boy come up there by the name of Emmett Harding. He was very good. And Emmett was playing with a band by the name of Brownlee, who was a bass player. And Brownlee was playing at a hall they called the Owl's Hall. They used to play all around too. In those days the bands would go from corner to corner playing. I could see this little boy setting on top of the piano, playing his cornet with his half a pint on the side of him. And I mean, he would make a variation front ways and turn around and play that thing backwards and man, that's as good as he played in front. That's how good he was now. And then in later years, him and Loey got hooked up on a steamboat out there. I think it was a steamer capital or a sydney. I don't know which one. I think it was a sydney myself. And Loey was on one end. He was playing with Fate Marvel, I think. I think he was playing with Fate. And this Brownlee band was on the other end. And I think Monk Hazel played in that band too with him. And then Loey started blowing at this boy. And this boy was mad. This boy started blowing back at him. And Loey bowed to him and said, Brother, you can play. And he says, You're better mad than I am. But the kid died young. And in the meantime, this is when Bix Spider-Bike came down here. And this kid taught Bix what he knew. And Bix to me took his style because this kid played two styles. He played the style Bix played and he played the style Loey played. And Bix was down here doing nothing. And he took this style back up north and made a lot of money with it. That's what I think about that kid. It was the most outstanding trumpet player down here at that time. Let it years and years come along like Red Bone was a fine trumpet band too. And different one, there was a colored boy there that played plenty trumpet down here too. He's dead and that's kid, Rene. And I say he could play as much trumpet as what Loey played. In fact, he played pretty Loey in those days.
You talked about Rene, and you were saying how good he was.

Yeah, Rene was... I remember Rene. When I was a young kid, I would just start, like I told you, I played in one key. And that was the trumpet player that I followed around the streets. Every time I'd see Rene, he was on some wagon playing for the fights or something like that. And they used to go from corner to corner. And there was one particular tune that I heard him play. And I liked that tune so well that I played that tune today myself. And every time I played, I always think about it Rene because he played it so pretty. It was a tune by the name of Hawaiian Skies. And I played it with such a beautiful tone. He used to use a little bitty mouthpiece, and he'd stick it on his lip there. And you couldn't even see the mouthpiece. You couldn't see the bell of it or nothing. Because his lips would go over the mouthpiece. But the most beautiful music came out of that horn. He used a little cornet, because it's the way I'm using now, a little fake tomorrow. And he used to play that tune, Hawaiian Skies. And played it beautiful, pretty. Rene had a style. He didn't make many variations. But the things that he played, played it pretty. And he played it good. And with that, he had a big tune. And I followed him around because I really thought in them days he was the best trumpet player. And then in the later years they had trumpet players that came on. While it was Buddy P. Teague. And then Sam Morgan's band. And uh... And uh... There was this piano player that played on a boat a while too. A good friend of mine. He played a daps in Us for a good while. I can't think of his...
Fats.

Fats P. Well, Fats was coming up around in them days. Many times I went to Fats' house. He and I used to get together on the piano and trumpet. That's how long I know Fats. There used to be another friend of mine by the name of Al Corliss that played piano. That's a good friend of mine. He's in Steamship business today. He was a fine piano player too. But we used to like Fats. We used to like to hear Fats play. So we'd go call up Fats and go down to his house. Sit around, drink some coffee and start jamming. I don't know. But, well, Fats played with all different bands in them days. I don't know if Fats played with, there used to be a violin player. It used to play out the lake years ago in a place called Tranchina. He had a nice band out there too for years. I can't think of that man's name now. He was on the end of my time. He was a very good...
Was that Peter Boccaz who was a corner player in that band?
Where, where? Out of the lake.
Do you know him? Real like that.
Oh, no.
I was thinking of Piron's band.
Piron's the band I'm thinking about. Yeah, that's the band I'm thinking about. Piron.
Well, how did those corner players you say in later years compare with people like Frank Christian and the real old timers from that era, before your time?

Oh, well, Frank Christian was a... I wouldn't have called him a... He was more of a straight man. Christian. Frank Christian was. He... He wasn't a... Compared to a man like... I'm gonna say, nah, nah, that's my view, viewpoint. I don't know, everybody thinks things different though, but you couldn't compare him with a man like... The boy we were just talking about, Kid Rene and Louie and Emmon Hart and trumpet players like that. You... He was in a different category, I'd say. I'd say, yeah. He was in a... Category like Nick LaRock, I'd say. You know, they played a different style of jazz than these men played. The style they played, we used to call that jazz ago, ragtime jazz. And... But that wasn't Dixieland, huh? I don't know, I don't think that was Dixieland because... It didn't have the style. I didn't think it was the style. I wouldn't call that... I'd call that ragtime the way they had the name foot in those days. It was ragtime jazz. And a man like Hardy and Rene and Sam Morgan and... Buck Johnson, King Oliver. All them fellas had a different style. I don't know, it was a style you would... A musician would like to hear. That's the style I liked. Some of them played corn style. Some of them played... Take Louis. The style he's playing today, I have records on where Louis satin in the middle of a corn band. But his style is the same way. And he was born with that style. And he never did change that style. So they all had different styles. Of course they called them ragtime musicians. I don't know, I just called them playing corn. So I wouldn't compare them fellas with these fellas. Of course I may be wrong, I don't know. That's the way that I felt about different musicians that I've heard and played. Of course I played with plenty of corn bands myself in them days. Because I just needed the money.
Well what about Lester Nelson? We were talking about him a minute ago.

Nelson, yeah. He was a fine tenor man. I say he was one of the best tenor men around him. And that was before Miller's time. Of course Miller got the credit later on. But I said Lester could outplay any of these fellas. And he played a nice style. And a likable style. He had a kind of a rolling style. He didn't tongue his notes. He just slaughtered them. It just came out from the heart I'd say.
Was he about your age?
Yeah, he was around my age. Well he was a little bit younger than me I think. But older than Miller? Older than Miller, yeah. More than in Charlie Cordillo's class?
Yeah.
No, not that old. But between that. You see I think Miller's around in his forties now. I think fifties now.
Fifty?
Maybe.
I don't know.

I don't know. I think in his late forties. And Lester's, Lester's been about in his middle fifties now. And, uh, him and, uh, was another good clarinet player. I was talking to him yesterday. These two boys used to team up. One time, three of them teamed up together. And, uh, with a boy named Jack Marano. Very good clarinet and, and sax man. And, uh, him and Lester and Harry Shields, it was the team up. Three of them played in the same joint at the same time. And the Vanity Club down on Boybin and, uh, Bienville. And, uh, I, I happened to be playing in that band too. And there was Angelo. And, uh, a boy named Joe Harris on, uh, piano. And, uh, uh, Rodgers on drums.
And, uh, which Angelo is this? The guitar player?

Angelo Pram, Pramensal. Yeah. He played guitar. And, uh, well, these, these three, three fellas teamed up together. And, uh, you talk about some wonderful harmony. Cause I know Shields was good in his harrow. And, uh, Jack Marano played, uh, tenor, double clarinet too with Shields. And, uh, uh, when the three of them played, uh, Jack was playing alto. And, uh, and, uh, and, uh, Shields and, uh, Lester Nelson was playing tenor. Man, they made a fine team up. I was a good band in them days. But, uh, all in all, they had some mighty good bands in them days. But nobody got a break in them days. Because those days, the, uh, music that we were playing in those days, people didn't think very much of it in those days. The way they think of it now. Now, if we'd have started out, if the people in those days would, uh, thought about it the way they'd think now, we'd have been millionaires, I'd say. Because we'd have went right to the top. But we were playing for three dollars a night. Two and a half a night. I only worked with Roy Zinnerman for a dollar and a half a night at the spotlight. He was another good man. He worked for a dollar and a half a night. Me. Jerry Cooper. Candy Candina. We all played together for a buck and a half a night at the spotlight.
Jerry Cooper?

Jerry Cooper, the singer. He's up, uh, he's up in New York. He left in and he never did come back. There was Jerry Cooper, myself, Candy Candina, uh, Coco, and, uh, Joe Valenti. He's playing bass now. And, uh, I don't know who was on the drums at that time. But that was in a spotlight. They had a night club in them days. Cabaret, they called them. That's what they called them in those days. Cabarets. And we were all playing in that same place for a dollar and a half a night. And if we'd have gotten a break that some of these musicians are fortunate enough to get today, I think we'd have all been on the top too. But it just came too late for a lot of us. That's the reason why we all washed up. And we were all playing in the middle of the night. Because it's too late in life to start over. That's what my view about the thing. And I say, if all these musicians that's coming up, these young ones, they just put their mind to, if, if they're gonna play Dixieland, they ought to try to stick to the lead mostly. Instead of trying to vary it all over the horn and the public don't know what they're playing. I often think if they'll stick to the lead, they'll wind up being better musicians. And playing all this kind of music that they want to play these days. I don't know. It just defeats me. I can't understand that maybe I'm in a different category. That's all. Times has changed, like I say. You know what I mean? Like the college students and all might go for progressive music these days. I don't know. And bebop and all. But that's not music to it. Somebody would've trained me. I said, I want to stick more around melody. I think they'd wind up better. My viewpoint of it is that I always liked to variate too. But I always did fall back on melody to find out where I was. Because sometimes you could be very varied on out in the clouds. So if you stare out at Leeds, you're gonna find out where you are. I think musicians these days, they always changing. I mean, I don't know. I guess they're just moving into another world.
Well I think the kids today like to hear melody. I think people still like melody and they like to dance.

I think so. They like to dance. Now I've played for a lot of teenagers already. And they've often told us that they like the band. Because we played a lot of stuff that they heard. And they knew about it, you know. And they like to hear that of course. There's a lot of them that we go out and play these days. They ask you to play rock and roll western. So you've got to learn how to play a little bit of everything. In order to satisfy the public these days. It's the way that I've been doing. If somebody wants me to play a samba, I'm gonna play a samba. I'm gonna play the samba that I know. The one that I can play. And I say that's the main thing about playing music for the public. Is to please the public. Try to play what they want you to play. Not play what you want. I see your friend here, Johnny Wiggs is in this picture here. This is our band there. Larry Shields too. Abby Brunus. Buegman Sam. This is Larry Shields here. Yeah, Larry Shields. This is a picture that was taken some time back in the second line. Connie, I wanted to ask you.
What tunes do you feature now that are sort of forgotten to most bands? Like Avalian Scots. I don't know anybody else but you and Raymond and I guess Paul.
That's right. Raymond knows that tune.
Down under beneath of Hawaii and Scotland.

It goes da da da da da da da da da da da da da. Raymond played that all the time. And I liked it too. Because Raymond heard it too when Rene played it. Now that's tunes that I played. And I always liked to play singing the blues. That was something pretty. I always played that. I never heard many bands play it. But I always featured a tune like that. Because it had beautiful harmony in it. And of course I couldn't have played it the way Biggs made it though. But I mean it was always a standard tune. And some of the old tunes, well I think I knew every Dixieland tune in a book. In fact, like Maple Leaf Rag. Well I never heard many bands around here play that tune. That's an old Dixieland tune. And ain't nobody ever did play it. But I always did play it. And that's tunes that I featured. Of course I play all the regular standards. That's been playing for years. Like Mood, Indigo. And things like River St. Marie. I like tunes. Beautiful. Yeah, beautiful tunes like that. Well you, you know if you've played Paul a lot of times with me. You know that I play a different rock and rock tunes that the other bands play. Because I always had different tunes in my brains all the time. Like I like Someday's Sweetheart. In fact, like the voice of it. I always did like to play the voice of that tune. I never did hear anybody play voices. But I always did like to play voices on tunes. And it makes it pretty, I don't know. I've had a lot of people, I was playing the voice and they come up there and they said, you play two tunes. What's the name of that other one? I said, no, that was the same tune. It was the voice of that tune. Why? Because their ear was just trained to hear that chorus. And I always thought that I would like to play something different than the other fella play. And then one time there, I, well I have a little ride up in here. One time Dutch and I was, had a bucking contest. Down at the circle. That was down on St. Claude and Allegiant Field. Well Dutch, Andrews and Tony and Dixie Ramblers. I won't forget that. And Dutch really thought he had the job sold up. Because he was playing there already. You see, the man says, well, I'm going to put a bucking contest on. The man that, that wins the contest stays here for the rest of the season. So Dutch was playing there already. He had all these friends there to pull for him. So I come up there cold turkey. With no friends. And we bucked and bucked for four hours that night. And come to find out Dutch lost the contest. And I got the job and I got the proof in there. The other one said.
I saw that circle.

Yeah. Well it proves to you that, uh, you, uh, never know why, why I, I, uh, wanted, because I was something different that night. I played something different. I didn't play anything he played. He played something, I come out with something. No. Well the things that I played that, that night, the people never heard them, maybe. And that's, that's what won the contest, I think. Of course it was a big deal in them days. I think, just to pay about $4 a night. That was big money. Uh, Elysian Field, uh, and, uh, St. Claude, uh, right, right away, it's sweeping the store. Uh, uh, Sharky and, uh, Leon Prima opened that place up the first time. It was Sharky and Prima's band. Them, uh, two were team, teamed up one time years ago. They had a modified band, Sharky and, and Prima. Oh, and they went along for a long time. Cause I, I, Sharky, I know Sharky man when, he was playing out at Millenburg in a place every Sunday out there. And, uh, I, I, I was, well, I wasn't even playing, you know, I, I used to go out there to hear him play. I used to give a big dance out there every Sunday. I used to catch a whole train out there, they call, uh, the, uh, Smoke, Smokey Mary they used to call. And we used to go out there every Sunday to hear the band. There used to be picnics out there all day long. And, uh, gee, that's way back in the 20s. 1919, I guess. Right back. I don't know Sharky. And, uh, they were a long time together and after that they split up. They only went one way and Sharky went another way. But, uh, Sharky was, was another man too. He was a fine trumpet player, but he, he positively didn't get no breaks either in them days. But, uh, he finally got his break in the later years. And, uh, in fact he was, was one of them, man, a few trumpet players that got a break like that. Because they had some mighty good trumpet players around there. But, uh, didn't get nowhere. They had to wind up, uh, uh, on, uh, streets working or driving a truck or like Red Bullman wind up being a plumber. I wind up being an insurance man. And, uh, wind up doing something because we couldn't make the living playing music like the boys that's coming up these days. And, uh, uh, a chance in life. You know what I said? Because, uh, they were younger and, uh, well, a musician's life's a funny life. You know that. You either make it or you don't make it. You either get the break, or when you get the break, that's the time you gotta take it. Now, I, I remember one time I had a chance to get a break, play up around Chicago. And, uh, and, uh, I, uh, wanted to go up there and play. But, but I was scared, so I came back home. Another time there, I, uh, finally joined this, this, this, this, uh, band out, out in, uh, Oklahoma. Shawnee, Oklahoma was a boy by the name of Brooks Pruitt on the piano. Joe Harris trombone. Sidney Howard and clarinet. Uh, uh, Roger Boyd on the drums. There was a fine band playing, uh, uh, dance hall music out there. Now, there was, those, those, those boys that I mentioned were, were, were stars. Today they are. Harris is, is, is a big time. Roger Boyd is, is, is a big time. I played some, some way. He was from Miami, some way. Uh, Brooks Pruitt was a fine piano player. Played with Gene Goldkett and different bands. Of course, he's, he's dead now. He got killed. But, uh, I played with bands like that though, but I always wanted to come home. I would get home sick. I wanna come home. So that was just the bad breaks that I got in life. But, I mean, if I'd have kept going forward, and, uh, thought about the home life. You know, I had a family to support and all that. I, uh, think if, if I was single, I went up the line and stayed up around there up until a break came. And I, thank God, I made a little money myself. I made a little change. I, uh, think, because I could play Dixieland if they wanted Dixieland. So I was a born faker. I never knew any music. The only time I learned the, the background of music. And later years, when I took lessons from a, a man by the name of Professor, uh, Dixieland D Music from the heart, I say. Jazz music. That's the only music I ever liked to play. Is there any question you'd like to ask me?
Yeah, I would like to know some more about that band that Sharky and Leon Prima had together. Who was in there with them?

Well, I think Shields was in that band, and Monk. I think Monk was back around in that band. And if it wasn't Monk, it was a barber named Leo Hadd. He was a fine drummer, and he died too. And I really don't know all the rest of them in that band. I can't think off, Hadd, but I know it is a mighty fine band. A very good band.
Remember the trombone player?
Oh yeah, that was old Julian Lane. He was a dead man. He was a man.
They were using two cornets back here then.

Yeah. Well, in the old days we used first and second trumpet, because many of the jobs that I played, I was always second trumpet man, and takeoff man, because the first man, the red. You know, I'm talking about the red bands.
You know?

But in those days, they played first and second trumpets in fake bands. I played with a fellow years ago by the name of Pete Dittra. He was the finest second trumpet man and first man, but it was strictly old fake music. Sometime I'd cattle eat, sometime I'd cattle eat, though. But with Glenn, years ago, that's all I did. I used two trumpets.
I think that's about it. So we're going to have to call it a day now.
That was good. Yeah. All right. Thank you a million bucks. Thank you.

segments.title: Opening identification and recording details
segments.summary: Allen gives the date, location and names for the recording; Tony Fougerat is identified.

segments.title: Born 1900, buying a cornet in 1918, Hotsy Totsy jam sessions
segments.summary: Fougerat wanted to be a locomotive engineer, bought a rusty cornet on Rampart Street, taught himself in the key of C, and later played jam sessions at the Hotsy Totsy c.1924.

segments.title: Lobosky, Max Finkman's group and its clarinetists
segments.summary: Allen asks about pianist Lobosky, who was a semi-jazz player with Max Finkman; they recall Red Bowman, Tony Parenti and a forgotten clarinetist's style.

segments.title: Bourbon Street clubs and leaving for vaudeville shows in 1928
segments.summary: He played Bourbon Street spots such as the Silver Slipper, then in 1928 joined presentation (vaudeville) shows.

segments.title: Photos of his New Orleans band with Jeff Riddick
segments.summary: Looking at a photograph, Fougerat names the band he had in New Orleans: Jeff Riddick, Billy Newburger, Al Bernard, Frank Topey, Marshall Farrell.

segments.title: Pontchartrain Beach band with Harry Shields, then back on the road
segments.summary: He fronted a band for years, then played Pontchartrain Beach with Harry Shields, Foster Petty, Zito and Stan Serge, before leaving again for tent shows with Jimmy Rogers.

segments.title: Tent shows, Hollywood Scandals and the Chicago circuit
segments.summary: Life on tent shows and week stands, Chicago and New York dates, a New England tour cancelled over union trouble, and the Collegiate band from Baton Rouge.

segments.title: A letter inviting his band to play a colored club
segments.summary: A funny letter from a Black club asking his WWL-broadcasting band to play a dance, which never happened.

segments.title: Family and being a paid 'dummy' in parade bands
segments.summary: His musical side comes from his mother's family; cousin Johnny Peugeot got him into parade bands where he filled out the numbers without playing.

segments.title: Chink Martin's group and the Dominoes at Woodman Hall
segments.summary: He recalls playing with Chink Martin, the Christian brothers and the Dominoes (Willie Guitars, Nappy Lamar, Tony Barella), for little pay.

segments.title: Willie Guitars' bass trap door and the Paul English Players tent show
segments.summary: A funny story about the drinking bassist's trap door, and about the six-piece band on the Paul English Players show.

segments.title: Buying the horn at twenty dollars and Jack Lane's band
segments.summary: Where and for how much he bought the horn at about age 18, and that Jack Lane was already going strong.

segments.title: Hardships of touring: 109 towns, unpaid shows and hunger
segments.summary: Long overnight jumps, a show that could not pay, chorus girls going hungry, and charging postage stamps to the hotel bill.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong, Emmett Harding and Bix Beiderbecke in New Orleans
segments.summary: He remembers Louis with King Oliver, the young cornetist Emmett Harding, a steamboat cutting contest, and his belief that Bix took his style from Harding; also Kid Rena.

segments.title: Kid Rene's beautiful tone and 'Hawaiian Skies'
segments.summary: He followed trumpeter Kid Rene around the streets as a youth and admired his tone and the tune Hawaiian Skies.

segments.title: Fats Pierce and Piron's band
segments.summary: Recollections of pianist Fats jamming at his house, friend Al Corliss, and a violinist at Tranchina's identified as Piron's band.

segments.title: Frank Christian and the old ragtime players compared with Rene and Louis
segments.summary: He judges the old ragtime-jazz men like Frank Christian against Rene, Louis, Sam Morgan and King Oliver, saying each had a different style.

segments.title: Lester Nelson and the ages of the tenor men
segments.summary: He praises tenor man Lester Nelson's rolling style and compares his age with Miller's.

segments.title: Vanity Club trio of Shields, Nelson and Jack Marano
segments.summary: Harry Shields, Lester Nelson and Jack Marano played together at the Vanity Club with Fougerat, Joe Harris, Angelo Pramensal and Rodgers.

segments.title: Low pay at the Spotlight cabaret and advice to young players
segments.summary: He recalls working for a dollar and a half a night at the Spotlight with Jerry Cooper and others, and says players should stick to the melody.

segments.title: Pleasing the audience and a second-line band photo
segments.summary: Agreeing that audiences like melody and dancing, he says a player must please the public; then points out Johnny Wiggs and Larry Shields in a photo.

segments.title: Forgotten tunes he features and playing the verse
segments.summary: He talks about Avalon, Singing the Blues, Maple Leaf Rag and playing verses of standards.

segments.title: Bucking contest with Dutch Andrus, Sharky, Oklahoma and bad breaks
segments.summary: He won a job at the Circle in a four-hour contest; tells of Sharky and Leon Prima, a Shawnee Oklahoma band, and why he never got a big break.

segments.title: Who played in Sharky and Leon Prima's band
segments.summary: Fougerat recalls Shields, Monk or drummer Leo Addy, and trombonist Julian Lane in that band.

segments.title: First and second trumpet in the old bands
segments.summary: He explains the old practice of first and second trumpet and that he mostly played second.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Allen ends the interview and they thank each other.
